title: PAPHR making changes due to Ballantyne death
article: With the inquest finished and recommendations made, the Prince Albert Parkland Health Region is very receptive to making changes.
"The health region, first of all, wants to express its condolences to the Ballantyne family and that we are very concerned about our patients and their families," PAPHR CEO Cecile Hunt said.
The inquest was looking into the death of William Leonard Ballantyne, who died on Nov. 29, 2012 at the Victoria Hospital.

Ballantyne was admitted into the hospital that day for severe back and abdominal pain. After it was assumed he was intoxicated and was being disruptive, Ballantyne was then taken into Prince Albert Police Service custody, before seeing a physician.

Later that morning, the police called paramedics to respond to Ballantyne, who was not breathing. The paramedics continued CPR on the way to the hospital, but Ballantyne didn't regain a heartbeat. He was pronounced dead at 10:13 a.m.
During an inquest held last week, a jury found the cause of Ballantyne's death to be an accidental acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose and made four recommendations, two in regards to PAPHR.

The first recommendation made to the health region was "due to excessive workloads the triage nurse be provided with an assistant to help meet the time guidelines for patient reassessment and quality of care."

Since testimony and documents showed Ballantyne "would have been in substantial pain during the time his liver was shutting down, and as a side effect would display characteristics of confusion similar to someone with dementia or Alzheimer's," lawyer for the family Kimberly Stonechild said in a news release.

If Ballantyne had been provided a more thorough examination, including a physical exam of his abdomen or taking blood or urine samples, the severity of his condition would have become apparent, according to forensic pathologist Dr. Shaun Ladham.
Hunt said the recommendation around excessive workloads is something the health region is very concerned about.

"We are looking at the existing resources within the emergency room to access our options there and if we need to we will have the access resources within the health region to ensure we can, that the triage nurse has adequate support," Hunt said. "The assistant option is certainly something that we are looking at very carefully."
PAPHR, along with the Saskatoon and Regina health regions, is part of a quality initiative around emergency room waits, Hunt said. They have already started doing work around wait times.
"We are actively looking at some of the areas that need improvement of which wait times are an area we are focused on," Hunt said. "A lot of our service line work is in this area already.

"Based on the results of our rapid process improvement initiatives, we are looking at options to support the triage nurse in making sure that our guidelines are being met," she added. "We have to look at our existing resources as well as other resources within the region to perhaps redirect them to this area."

The second recommendation stated "prior to contacting police to deal with anyone that is being disruptive or disorderly on hospital grounds, hospital security is to first consult with a medical practitioner.

In a news release from Prince Albert Grand Council,Chief Edward Henderson of Montreal Lake First Nation said the system failed Ballantyne when he was removed from the hospital at the discretion of the security guards.

"It's clear that Billy didn't receive the proper care he should've received when he first went to the hospital, and I recognize there is much work to be done to ensure that one's personal history or physical appearance does not play into the treatment of someone seeking medical help," Henderson said.
Hunt said they are already starting to take steps to make sure something similar to this situation doesn't happen again.

"We have already instituted some new guidelines ... that occurred shortly after the death of Mr. Ballantyne," Hunt said. "We now have our patients cleared by a physician before they leave the hospital premises due to many different reasons. That has been already implemented."
The health region conducted an internal review of Ballantyne's death and deemed it "a critical incident," Hunt said.

"We certainly recognize that there were lots of areas of improvement there and that did occur. It has been altered for a period of time," she said. "I think that we need to look at wait times that patients are having to wait at our hospital and see where we can improve. We need to learn from Mr. Ballantyne's death and we really do want to provide the best care possible."
